1.note: Tearing his **clothes** and wearing **sackcloth** were symbolic actions by which King Hezekiah showed that he was deeply distressed. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And when Hezekiah heard the words of Rabshakeh, the king grabbed his own clothes and tore them into two pieces to show his grief]
Isaiah is speaking of the temple of Yahweh as if it were a **house** in which he lived. Alternate translation: [into the temple of Yahweh]

2.q: וַ֠⁠יִּשְׁלַח אֶת־אֶלְיָקִ֨ים אֲשֶׁר־עַל־הַ⁠בַּ֜יִת וְ⁠אֵ֣ת שֶׁבְנָ֣א הַ⁠סּוֹפֵ֗ר
2.note: Translate the names of these men the same as you did in Isaiah 36:3.
This is an idiom that means that Eliakim was in charge of the affairs of the palace household. Alternate translation: [Eliakim, who was in charge of the palace]

3.q: וַ⁠יֹּאמְר֣וּ אֵלָ֗י⁠ו כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר חִזְקִיָּ֔הוּ יוֹם־צָרָ֧ה וְ⁠תוֹכֵחָ֛ה וּ⁠נְאָצָ֖ה הַ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה כִּ֣י בָ֤אוּ בָנִים֙ עַד־מַשְׁבֵּ֔ר וְ⁠כֹ֥חַ אַ֖יִן לְ⁠לֵדָֽה
3.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Hezekiah says that this day is a day of trouble and chastisement and reproach, for sons have come to the birth canal, but there is no strength to give birth]

3.q: כִּ֣י בָ֤אוּ בָנִים֙ עַד־מַשְׁבֵּ֔ר וְ⁠כֹ֥חַ אַ֖יִן לְ⁠לֵדָֽה
3.note: Hezekiah is using or inventing a proverb in order to illustrate that the Judeans are in a life-and-death situation, but they do not have the resources to rescue themselves from it. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture.

4.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. In many languages it will not be necessary to make significant alterations. Alternate translation: [Hezekiah says that perhaps Yahweh your God will have heard]

Isaiah is using the term **words** to represent what Rabshakeh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everything that the Rabshakeh said]

4.q: וְ⁠הוֹכִ֨יחַ֙ בַּ⁠דְּבָרִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר שָׁמַ֖ע יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֑י⁠ךָ
4.note: Since the author has already used the name Yahweh earlier in this sentence, it may be more natural in your language to use a pronoun here. Alternate translation: [and he will chastise the words that he has heard]

4.q: וְ⁠הוֹכִ֨יחַ֙ בַּ⁠דְּבָרִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר שָׁמַ֖ע יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֑י⁠ךָ
4.note: The messengers are using the **words** that the Rabshakeh spoke to represent the Rabshakeh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and he will chastise him for what he heard him say]

The messengers are speaking as if a **prayer** were something that Isaiah could physically **lift up**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And may you say a prayer]

Isaiah is using **the remnant that is found** as a common expression of the culture to mean “those who remain alive.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the remnant of Judeans who still survive]

5.note: In this verse, the author is describing an event after describing in the previous two verses an event that followed it. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened. You could do that by putting this sentence at the start of verse 3. You could also translate this verse in such a way as to show that this event preceded the events of the previous two verses and begin verse 6 with “then.” Alternate translation: [And when the servants of King Hezekiah had come to Isaiah]

6.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר אֲלֵי⁠הֶם֙ יְשַֽׁעְיָ֔הוּ כֹּ֥ה תֹאמְר֖וּ⁠ן אֶל־אֲדֹנֵי⁠כֶ֑ם כֹּ֣ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה אַל־תִּירָא֙ מִ⁠פְּנֵ֤י הַ⁠דְּבָרִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁמַ֔עְתָּ אֲשֶׁ֧ר גִּדְּפ֛וּ נַעֲרֵ֥י מֶלֶךְ־אַשּׁ֖וּר אוֹתִֽ⁠י
6.note: There are three levels of quotation in this verse. The author is quoting what **Isaiah** said (level 1). Isaiah tells Hezekiah’s officials what he wants them to say to their **master** Hezekiah (level 2). This includes a quotation from **Yahweh** (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation, here and at the end of the next verse. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

6.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר אֲלֵי⁠הֶם֙ יְשַֽׁעְיָ֔הוּ כֹּ֥ה תֹאמְר֖וּ⁠ן אֶל־אֲדֹנֵי⁠כֶ֑ם כֹּ֣ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה אַל־תִּירָא֙ מִ⁠פְּנֵ֤י הַ⁠דְּבָרִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁמַ֔עְתָּ אֲשֶׁ֧ר גִּדְּפ֛וּ נַעֲרֵ֥י מֶלֶךְ־אַשּׁ֖וּר אוֹתִֽ⁠י
6.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and Isaiah told them to tell Hezekiah that Yahweh said he should not be afraid from the face of the words that he had heard, by which the servants of the king of Assyria had blasphemed him]

Yahweh is using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on behalf of] or [because of]

Isaiah uses a specific word for **servants** that in other contexts can mean a “young man” or “boy.” While Hezekiah told his officials to refer to the Rabshakeh by his official title, Isaiah is belittling the Assyrian officials. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [the lackeys of the king of Assyria]

7.q: הִנְ⁠נִ֨י נוֹתֵ֥ן בּ⁠וֹ֙ ר֔וּחַ וְ⁠שָׁמַ֥ע שְׁמוּעָ֖ה וְ⁠שָׁ֣ב אֶל־אַרְצ֑⁠וֹ וְ⁠הִפַּלְתִּ֥י⁠ו בַּ⁠חֶ֖רֶב בְּ⁠אַרְצֽ⁠וֹ
7.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be quotations within a quotations, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [Tell Hezekiah that Yahweh says that he is about to put a spirit on the king of Assyria, and he will hear a report, and he will return to his land, and Yahweh will make him fall by the sword in his land]

Yahweh is using a common expression of this culture, **Behold me**, to indicate that he is about to do something. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 2 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 2 Samuel 12:11. Alternate translation: [I am about to put]

8.q: וַ⁠יָּ֨שָׁב֙ רַב־שָׁקֵ֔ה וַ⁠יִּמְצָא֙ אֶת־מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר נִלְחָ֖ם עַל־לִבְנָ֑ה כִּ֣י שָׁמַ֔ע כִּ֥י נָסַ֖ע מִ⁠לָּכִֽישׁ
8.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and since he had heard that the king of Assyria had departed from Lachish, he found him fighting against Libnah]

The author does not mean that the Rabshakeh had to look for the **king of Assyria** and that he **found him** at **Libnah**. He means that he met him there. See how you translated the similar expression in 9:21. Alternate translation: [and he met]

The pronoun **he** refers in the first instance to **the Rabshakeh**, and in the second instance, **he** refers to **the king of Assyria**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Rabshakeh had heard that the king had departed from Lachish]

9.note: The first use of the pronoun **he** refers to the king of Assyria. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Then the king of Assyria heard]

The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly. Alternate translation: [and instructing messengers what to say to Hezekiah, he told them]

10.q: כֹּ֣ה תֹאמְר֗וּ⁠ן אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֤הוּ מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָה֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר אַל־יַשִּֽׁאֲ⁠ךָ֣ אֱלֹהֶ֔י⁠ךָ אֲשֶׁ֥ר אַתָּ֛ה בּוֹטֵ֥חַ בּ֖⁠וֹ לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר לֹ֤א תִנָּתֵן֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם בְּ⁠יַ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
10.note: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the long quotation in verses 10–13. There are three levels of quotation in this verse. The author is quoting what the king of Assyria said to his messengers (level 1). The king is telling his messengers what he wants them to say to Hezekiah (level 2). This includes a quotation of something that the Assyrian king believes Yahweh is telling Hezekiah (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

10.q: כֹּ֣ה תֹאמְר֗וּ⁠ן אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֤הוּ מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָה֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר אַל־יַשִּֽׁאֲ⁠ךָ֣ אֱלֹהֶ֔י⁠ךָ אֲשֶׁ֥ר אַתָּ֛ה בּוֹטֵ֥חַ בּ֖⁠וֹ לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר לֹ֤א תִנָּתֵן֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם בְּ⁠יַ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
10.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there are not quotations within a quotations. Alternate translation: [Tell Hezekiah, the king of Judah, that he should not let his God, in whom he is trusting, deceive him by telling him that Jerusalem will not be given into my hand]

10.q: לֹ֤א תִנָּתֵן֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם בְּ⁠יַ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
10.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 36:15. Alternate translation: [I will not give Jerusalem into the control of the king of Assyria] or [I will not allow the king of Assyria to conquer Jerusalem]

11.q: הִנֵּ֣ה ׀ אַתָּ֣ה שָׁמַ֗עְתָּ אֲשֶׁ֨ר עָשׂ֜וּ מַלְכֵ֥י אַשּׁ֛וּר לְ⁠כָל־הָ⁠אֲרָצ֖וֹת לְ⁠הַחֲרִימָ֑⁠ם וְ⁠אַתָּ֖ה תִּנָּצֵֽל
11.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Remind him that he has personally heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all of the lands by destroying them. Tell him there is no reason why he should expect that, by contrast, his God will deliver him]

The king of Assyria is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you have heard** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Hezekiah himself has already heard this news. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [you have heard personally]

The king is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. He is referring specifically to **to all of the lands** that the Assyrians have so far invaded. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [to every single one of the lands they have attacked]

The pronoun **you** is used here for emphasis, contrasting Hezekiah with the nations that were destroyed. Alternate translation: [So will you, by contrast, be delivered] or [So for your part, will you be delivered]

The expression **will you be delivered** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [So, by contrast, will Yahweh deliver you]

The king of Assyria is using the question form to emphasize that he does not believe that Yahweh will deliver Hezekiah. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [So do not think that you will be delivered.] or [So do not think that Yahweh will deliver you!]

12.q: הַ⁠הִצִּ֨ילוּ אוֹתָ֜⁠ם אֱלֹהֵ֤י הַ⁠גּוֹיִם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הִשְׁחִ֣יתוּ אֲבוֹתַ֔⁠י אֶת־גּוֹזָ֖ן וְ⁠אֶת־חָרָ֑ן וְ⁠רֶ֥צֶף וּ⁠בְנֵי־עֶ֖דֶן אֲשֶׁ֥ר בִּ⁠תְלַשָּֽׂר
12.note: The Assyrian king is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The gods of the nations that my fathers destroyed, Gozan and Haran and Rezeph and the sons of Eden who were in Tel Assar, did not deliver any of them!]

12.q: הַ⁠הִצִּ֨ילוּ אוֹתָ֜⁠ם אֱלֹהֵ֤י הַ⁠גּוֹיִם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הִשְׁחִ֣יתוּ אֲבוֹתַ֔⁠י אֶת־גּוֹזָ֖ן וְ⁠אֶת־חָרָ֑ן וְ⁠רֶ֥צֶף וּ⁠בְנֵי־עֶ֖דֶן אֲשֶׁ֥ר בִּ⁠תְלַשָּֽׂר
12.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Remind Hezekiah that the gods of the nations that my fathers destroyed did not deliver them, Gozan and Haran and Rezeph and the sons of Eden who were in Tel Assar.]
The Assyrian king is using the word **fathers** to mean his ancestors. Alternate translation: [my ancestors]
The expression **sons of Eden** refers to the people who lived in the region of Eden. Alternate translation: [the Edenites]

13.q: אַיֵּ֤ה מֶֽלֶךְ־חֲמָת֙ וּ⁠מֶ֣לֶךְ אַרְפָּ֔ד וּ⁠מֶ֖לֶךְ לָעִ֣יר סְפַרְוָ֑יִם הֵנַ֖ע וְ⁠עִוָּֽה
13.note: The king of Assyria is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The kings of Hamath and Arpad and of the cities of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah are all gone!]

13.q: אַיֵּ֤ה מֶֽלֶךְ־חֲמָת֙ וּ⁠מֶ֣לֶךְ אַרְפָּ֔ד וּ⁠מֶ֖לֶךְ לָעִ֣יר סְפַרְוָ֑יִם הֵנַ֖ע וְ⁠עִוָּֽה
13.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Remind Hezekiah that Assyrians defeated the kings of Hamath and Arpad and of the cities of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah, so all those kings no longer rule.]

In this expression, the words **king** and **city** are singular in form, but they refers to the kings of all three of the cities listed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural forms in your translation. Alternate translation: [or the kings of the cities of Sepharvaim, Hena, or Ivvah]

14.q: וַ⁠יִּקַּ֨ח חִזְקִיָּ֧הוּ אֶת־הַ⁠סְּפָרִ֛ים מִ⁠יַּ֥ד הַ⁠מַּלְאָכִ֖ים וַ⁠יִּקְרָאֵ֑⁠הוּ
14.note: While the term **writings** is plural, the author’s use of the singular pronoun **it** in the next clause and the next sentence shows that Hezekiah received one letter from the king of Assyria. (His messengers apparently read the contents of this letter out loud to Hezekiah and then gave him the written copy of the message for confirmation.) So in this context, the term **writings** has the sense of “the things that the king had written.” You could indicate that explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. You could also use singular forms instead of plural ones. Alternate translation: [Then the messengers handed Hezekiah a written copy of what they had said, and he read the things that the king had written] or [Then Hezekiah took the letter from the hand of the messengers, and he read it]

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, Isaiah is marking travel for change in elevation, **up**. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [And he went]

When Hezekiah **spread** the letter **out** (unrolled the scroll on which it was written) so that the contents were visible to Yahweh, this was a symbolic action by which he was asking for help by calling Yahweh’s attention to what Sennacherib had written, specifically the claim that Yahweh was no different from the gods of other nations. (Hezekiah did not believe that Yahweh would not know what was in the letter if he did not unroll the scroll. Also, Sennacherib’s messengers had stated the contents out loud before giving him this written version.) If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and Hezekiah spread it out before Yahweh as an appeal for help]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of Yahweh] or [where Yahweh could see it]

15.note: Here, **saying** represents the words of Hezekiah’s prayer that follow. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And Hezekiah prayed to Yahweh with these words]
See how you decided to represent the phrase **saying** when it introduces a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [and he said]

16.note: Hezekiah is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **made** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that God alone was the maker of **the heavens and the earth**. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [You, only you, made the heavens and the earth]

17.note: Hezekiah is speaking as if he wants Yahweh physically to **Incline** his **ear**, that is, to lean over the way someone would do to listen closely to someone who was located below him, such as a supplicant who was kneeling in front of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Listen carefully]

17.q: הַטֵּ֨ה יְהוָ֤ה אָזְנְ⁠ךָ֙ וּֽ⁠שְׁמָ֔ע פְּקַ֧ח יְהוָ֛ה עֵינֶ֖⁠ךָ וּ⁠רְאֵ֑ה וּ⁠שְׁמַ֗ע
17.note: The phrases **Incline your ear**, **hear**, **Open your eyes**, **see**, and **hear** an imperatives, but they communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please incline your ear, Yahweh, and hear. Please open your eyes, Yahweh, and see. And please hear]

18.note: In this verse, the word **land** is singular in form, but it refers to all of the lands of these **nations** as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “land.” Alternate translation: [and their lands]

19.q: וְ⁠נָתֹ֥ן אֶת־אֱלֹהֵי⁠הֶ֖ם בָּ⁠אֵ֑שׁ כִּי֩ לֹ֨א אֱלֹהִ֜ים הֵ֗מָּה כִּ֣י אִם־מַעֲשֵׂ֧ה יְדֵֽי־אָדָ֛ם עֵ֥ץ וָ⁠אֶ֖בֶן וַֽ⁠יְאַבְּדֽוּ⁠ם
19.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And since their gods are not gods, but rather the work of the hands of man, wood and stone, they have put them in the fire and destroyed them]

Hezekiah is using one part of people, their **hands**, to mean all of them in the act of making **gods** out of **wood** and **stone**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the work of craftsmen]

20.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 5:3 and 5:5.

Here, **hand** represents the power/control/capability of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from his power]

21.q: לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֲשֶׁר֙ הִתְפַּלַּ֣לְתָּ אֵלַ֔⁠י אֶל־סַנְחֵרִ֖יב מֶ֥לֶךְ אַשּֽׁוּר
21.note: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the long quotation in verses 21–35, in which there are multiple levels of quotation. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this verse so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [telling him that Yahweh, the God of Israel, said that he had heard what he had prayed to him about Sennacherib, the king of Assyria]

22.q: זֶ֣ה הַ⁠דָּבָ֔ר אֲשֶׁר־דִּבֶּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה עָלָ֑י⁠ו בָּזָ֨ה לְ⁠ךָ֜ לָעֲגָ֣ה לְ⁠ךָ֗ בְּתוּלַת֙ בַּת־צִיּ֔וֹן אַחֲרֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ רֹ֣אשׁ הֵנִ֔יעָה בַּ֖ת יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם
22.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [This is the word that Yahweh has spoken about him. He says that the virgin, the daughter of Zion, despises him, she derides him. The daughter of Jerusalem shakes a head after him]

22.q: בָּזָ֨ה לְ⁠ךָ֜ לָעֲגָ֣ה לְ⁠ךָ֗ בְּתוּלַת֙ בַּת־צִיּ֔וֹן אַחֲרֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ רֹ֣אשׁ הֵנִ֔יעָה בַּ֖ת יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם
22.note: Isaiah is speaking as if the city of **Jerusalem** were actually a mother and its inhabitants were her **daughter**. (In the first instance of this image, he uses the term **Zion**, the mountain on which the city was located, to represent the city itself.) If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The people of Jerusalem despise you, they deride you. The people of Jerusalem shake their heads after you]

22.q: בָּזָ֨ה לְ⁠ךָ֜ לָעֲגָ֣ה לְ⁠ךָ֗ בְּתוּלַת֙ בַּת־צִיּ֔וֹן אַחֲרֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ רֹ֣אשׁ הֵנִ֔יעָה בַּ֖ת יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם
22.note: Isaiah is using the present tense to describe something that is going to happen in the future in order to show that it will certainly happen and that it will happen soon. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use the future tense. Alternate translation: [The people of Jerusalem will despise you, they will deride you. The people of Jerusalem will shake their heads after you]

22.q: בָּזָ֨ה לְ⁠ךָ֜ לָעֲגָ֣ה לְ⁠ךָ֗ בְּתוּלַת֙ בַּת־צִיּ֔וֹן אַחֲרֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ רֹ֣אשׁ הֵנִ֔יעָה בַּ֖ת יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם
22.note: Yahweh, speaking through Isaiah, is speaking to someone whom he knows cannot hear him, the king of Assyria. He is doing this to communicate to Hezekiah that he feels very strongly about that king’s arrogance and mockery. If it would be helpful in your language, here and through verse 28, you could translate these words as if Yahweh were speaking directly to Hezekiah about the king of Assyria. Alternate translation: [The virgin, the daughter of Zion, despises him, she derides him. The daughter of Jerusalem shakes her head after him] or [The people of Jerusalem will despise him, they will deride him. The people of Jerusalem will shake their heads after him]

In this culture, shaking or wagging one’s head at a person was a symbolic action by which people showed contempt and expressed mockery toward that person. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [The daughter will shake her head disdainfully and mockingly after you]

Isaiah assumes that his listeners will know that by **after you**, he means that the Assyrians will flee from Jerusalem and that the people of the city will make this gesture at them as they run away. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at you as you flee] or [at him as he flees]

23.q: אֶת־מִ֤י חֵרַ֨פְתָּ֙ וְ⁠גִדַּ֔פְתָּ וְ⁠עַל־מִ֖י הֲרִימ֣וֹתָה קּ֑וֹל וַ⁠תִּשָּׂ֥א מָר֛וֹם עֵינֶ֖י⁠ךָ אֶל־קְד֥וֹשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
23.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh asks Sennacherib whom he has mocked and taunted. Yahweh asks him against whom he has raised a voice and lifted his eyes upward. The answer is that Sennacherib has done that against him, the Holy One of Israel!]

23.q: אֶת־מִ֤י חֵרַ֨פְתָּ֙ וְ⁠גִדַּ֔פְתָּ וְ⁠עַל־מִ֖י הֲרִימ֣וֹתָה קּ֑וֹל וַ⁠תִּשָּׂ֥א מָר֛וֹם עֵינֶ֖י⁠ךָ
23.note: Yahweh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [You must realize whom have you mocked and taunted! You must realize against whom have you raised a voice and lifted your eyes upward!]

The action of **lifting** his **eyes upward** was a symbolic action by which the king of Assyria showed arrogance and defiance toward Yahweh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and arrogantly lifted your eyes upward] or [and defiantly lifted your eyes upward]

Yahweh is using this possessive form to describe the holy God with whom the Israelites are in a covenant relationship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the holy God with whom you Israelites are in a covenant relationship]

24.q: בְּ⁠יַ֣ד עֲבָדֶי⁠ךָ֮ חֵרַ֣פְתָּ ׀ אֲדֹנָ⁠י֒ וַ⁠תֹּ֗אמֶר בְּ⁠רֹ֥ב רִכְבִּ֛⁠י אֲנִ֥י עָלִ֛יתִי מְר֥וֹם הָרִ֖ים יַרְכְּתֵ֣י לְבָנ֑וֹן וְ⁠אֶכְרֹ֞ת קוֹמַ֤ת אֲרָזָי⁠ו֙ מִבְחַ֣ר בְּרֹשָׁ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠אָבוֹא֙ מְר֣וֹם קִצּ֔⁠וֹ יַ֖עַר כַּרְמִלּֽ⁠וֹ
24.note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what Isaiah told Hezekiah in his message (level 1), continuing from the previous verses. This includes what, according to Isaiah, Yahweh was saying to Hezekiah, also continuing from the previous verse (level 2). This includes a quotation from the king of Assyria (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

24.q: בְּ⁠יַ֣ד עֲבָדֶי⁠ךָ֮ חֵרַ֣פְתָּ ׀ אֲדֹנָ⁠י֒ וַ⁠תֹּ֗אמֶר בְּ⁠רֹ֥ב רִכְבִּ֛⁠י אֲנִ֥י עָלִ֛יתִי מְר֥וֹם הָרִ֖ים יַרְכְּתֵ֣י לְבָנ֑וֹן וְ⁠אֶכְרֹ֞ת קוֹמַ֤ת אֲרָזָי⁠ו֙ מִבְחַ֣ר בְּרֹשָׁ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠אָבוֹא֙ מְר֣וֹם קִצּ֔⁠וֹ יַ֖עַר כַּרְמִלּֽ⁠וֹ
24.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that by the hand of his servants he mocked him and said boastfully that with the multitude of his chariotry, he went up to the height of the mountains, the recesses of Lebanon. He boasted that he cut down the heights of its cedars, the choicest of its cypress trees, that he might enter the height of its end, the forest of its orchard]

24.q: בְּ⁠רֹ֥ב רִכְבִּ֛⁠י אֲנִ֥י עָלִ֛יתִי מְר֥וֹם הָרִ֖ים יַרְכְּתֵ֣י לְבָנ֑וֹן וְ⁠אֶכְרֹ֞ת קוֹמַ֤ת אֲרָזָי⁠ו֙ מִבְחַ֣ר בְּרֹשָׁ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠אָבוֹא֙ מְר֣וֹם קִצּ֔⁠וֹ יַ֖עַר כַּרְמִלּֽ⁠וֹ
24.note: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the elaborate comparison that the Assyrian king is drawing in this verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I commanded my chariot forces and invaded this land, even though it was remote from me and secure. I defeated the most powerful and skillful opponents. Now I am going to enter Jerusalem and capture the royal palace and temple]
Isaiah uses the word **servants** to mean the agency or authority of the servants. Alternate translation: [Through the agency of your servants]

The Assyrian king is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I went up** already includes this meaning. He is doing that for emphasis because he is boasting. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and said boastfully, “With the multitude of my chariotry, I myself went up]

25.q: אֲנִ֥י קַ֖רְתִּי וְ⁠שָׁתִ֣יתִי מָ֑יִם וְ⁠אַחְרִב֙ בְּ⁠כַף־פְּעָמַ֔⁠י כֹּ֖ל יְאֹרֵ֥י מָצֽוֹר
25.note: This verse is the conclusion of the third-level quotation that begins in the previous verse. If you have decided to use punctuation to mark levels of quotation, end this verse with the appropriate punctuation for closing a third-level quotation.

25.q: אֲנִ֥י קַ֖רְתִּי וְ⁠שָׁתִ֣יתִי מָ֑יִם וְ⁠אַחְרִב֙ בְּ⁠כַף־פְּעָמַ֔⁠י כֹּ֖ל יְאֹרֵ֥י מָצֽוֹר
25.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that the Assyrian king has boasted that he has dug wells and drunk waters. He has also boasted that he will dry up all of the streams of Matsor with the sole of his feet]

The Assyrian king is stating the pronoun **I** explicitly, even though the verb translated as **I dug** already includes this meaning, because he is boasting. See how you translated the similar expression in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [I myself dug, and I drank the waters]

The Assyrian king could be saying: (1) that he was able to dig wells and drink water from them in foreign countries. This would be a boast that his armies could successfully traverse arid, desolate areas. Alternate translation: [I have dug wells and drunk water from them] or (2) that he was able to dig wells and find water in places where no one suspected it would be. This might be a taunt at Hezekiah, who, according to 2 Chronicles 32:3–4, tried to eliminate the supply of water around the city of Jerusalem to thwart the Assyrians. Alternate translation: [I have been able to dig wells and find water in places my enemies did not expect]

The word **Matsor** is another name for Egypt. (The word is related to the word for “border.” Egypt was considered the border of Israel.) Alternate translation: [And with the sole of my feet I will dry up all of the streams of Egypt]

In this verse, the word **sole** is singular in form, but the king is using it to refer to both of his feet. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural or dual form of “sole.” Alternate translation: [And with the soles of my feet I will dry up all of the streams of Egypt]

The king is speaking as if he could actually **dry up all the streams of** Egypt with the soles of his **feet**, the way a person could stamp out a small puddle. The **streams** of Egypt, meaning the Nile and its tributary, represent something formidable, like the giant trees of Lebanon in the previous verse. The king is boasting that after conquering Jerusalem, he will conquer the Egyptian empire without great effort. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And next I will conquer Egypt without great effort]

26.q: הֲ⁠לֽוֹא־שָׁמַ֤עְתָּ לְ⁠מֵֽ⁠רָחוֹק֙ אוֹתָ֣⁠הּ עָשִׂ֔יתִי מִ֥⁠ימֵי קֶ֖דֶם וִ⁠יצַרְתִּ֑י⁠הָ עַתָּ֣ה הֲבֵאתִ֔י⁠הָ וּ⁠תְהִ֗י לְ⁠הַשְׁא֛וֹת גַּלִּ֥ים נִצִּ֖ים עָרִ֥ים בְּצֻרֽוֹת
26.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that the Assyrian king must surely have heard that from long ago, he did it; that from days of antiquity, he formed it. Now Yahweh has brought it, that the king should be for devastating fortified cities into ruined heaps]

26.q: הֲ⁠לֽוֹא־שָׁמַ֤עְתָּ לְ⁠מֵֽ⁠רָחוֹק֙ אוֹתָ֣⁠הּ עָשִׂ֔יתִי מִ֥⁠ימֵי קֶ֖דֶם וִ⁠יצַרְתִּ֑י⁠הָ
26.note: Yahweh is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Surely you must have heard that from long ago, I did it; that from days of antiquity, I formed it]

26.q: לְ⁠מֵֽ⁠רָחוֹק֙ אוֹתָ֣⁠הּ עָשִׂ֔יתִי מִ֥⁠ימֵי קֶ֖דֶם וִ⁠יצַרְתִּ֑י⁠הָ
26.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I decided a long time ago that this would happen]
Yahweh is using the term **days of antiquity** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from ancient times]

The expression **ruined** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [into heaps of ruins]

27.q: וְ⁠יֹֽשְׁבֵי⁠הֶן֙ קִצְרֵי־יָ֔ד חַ֖תּוּ וָ⁠בֹ֑שׁוּ הָי֞וּ עֵ֤שֶׂב שָׂדֶה֙ וִ֣⁠ירַק דֶּ֔שֶׁא חֲצִ֣יר גַּגּ֔וֹת וּ⁠שְׁדֵמָ֖ה לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י קָמָֽה
27.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that their dwellers are short of hand, they feel dismay and feel shame. They are vegetation of the field or green of herb; grass of roofs, blasting to the face of growing up]

Yahweh is using **short of hand** as a common expression of this culture to mean “powerless.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are powerless]

27.q: הָי֞וּ עֵ֤שֶׂב שָׂדֶה֙ וִ֣⁠ירַק דֶּ֔שֶׁא חֲצִ֣יר גַּגּ֔וֹת וּ⁠שְׁדֵמָ֖ה לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י קָמָֽה
27.note: Yahweh is speaking as if the people whom the Assyrians are conquering are actually tender plants that are defenseless against certain threats. Plants growing in the **field** can be easily trampled, for example, while **grass** growing on the flat **roofs** of this culture could easily wither in the heat of the sun. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They are as defenseless before the Assyrians as vegetation or green herbs out in the field or as grass on a flat roof, which withers in the heat of the sun]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe an **herb** that is characterized by being **green**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [or green herbs]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of the sun. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [grass on roofs, which the sun blasts before it can grow up]

28.q: וְ⁠שִׁבְתְּ⁠ךָ֛ וְ⁠צֵאתְ⁠ךָ֥ וּ⁠בוֹאֲ⁠ךָ֖ יָדָ֑עְתִּי וְ⁠אֵ֖ת הִֽתְרַגֶּזְ⁠ךָ֥ אֵלָֽ⁠י
28.note: If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [But Yahweh says he knows the dwelling of the king of Assyria and his going out and his coming in and his raging against him]

28.q: וְ⁠שִׁבְתְּ⁠ךָ֛ וְ⁠צֵאתְ⁠ךָ֥ וּ⁠בוֹאֲ⁠ךָ֖ יָדָ֑עְתִּי וְ⁠אֵ֖ת הִֽתְרַגֶּזְ⁠ךָ֥ אֵלָֽ⁠י
28.note: Yahweh is using two different conditions, either being at home or leaving or returning, to represent all conditions that the king of Assyria might be in. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [But I know everything about you, including how you rage against me]

29.note: The second-level quotation that begins in verse 21, in which Yahweh addresses the king of Assyria even though he cannot hear him, ends with this verse. If you have decided to use punctuation to mark levels of quotation, end this verse with the appropriate punctuation for closing a second-level quotation.

If you have decided to translate all of this long quotation in such a way that there will not be quotations within quotations, you can continue doing that in this verse. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that because of his raging against him and because his arrogance has come up into his ears, Yahweh will put his hook in the king’s nose and his bit in the king’s lips. And he will make him return on the way by which he came]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and because your arrogance has come up into my ears]

Here, **ears** represent hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and your arrogance has come up into my hearing] or [and I have heard from heaven the arrogant things you have been saying]

Yahweh is speaking as if he were actually going to put a **hook** in the **nose** of the king of Assyria and a **bit** in his **lips**, as if the king were an animal such as people would control by these means. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will control you by powerful means, and I will make you return on the way by which you came]
Here, the king’s **lips** represent his mouth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your mouth]

30.note: Isaiah is now addressing Hezekiah directly. He is no longer speaking in the first person on behalf of Yahweh (although he will do that again in verses 32–34). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And this will be the sign for you, Hezekiah]

If your language would not represent number in forms such as **second** or **third**, you could represent these numbers in forms that your language would use. Alternate translation: [and in year two, its offspring. But in year three] or [and next year, its offspring. But in the year after that]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [you will eat its offspring] or [you will eat what grows from that]

31.q: וְ⁠יָ֨סְפָ֜ה פְּלֵיטַ֧ת בֵּית־יְהוּדָ֛ה הַ⁠נִּשְׁאָרָ֖ה שֹׁ֣רֶשׁ לְ⁠מָ֑טָּה וְ⁠עָשָׂ֥ה פְרִ֖י לְ⁠מָֽעְלָ⁠ה
31.note: Isaiah is speaking as if the Judeans were actually a plant that would **{take} root** and **make fruit**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the Judeans who have survived and remain will establish themselves in their land again and have many children]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **survival**, you could express the same idea in another way, here and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [And the remaining survivors of the house of Judah]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Judah** figuratively means all the people descended from Judah, one of the sons of Israel. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Judah]

32.note: Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and survivors will come out from Mount Zion]

Some ancient manuscripts read “The zeal of Yahweh of armies will do this.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “The zeal of Yahweh will do this.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

Isaiah is speaking of the **zeal** of Yahweh as if it were a living thing that could do the things he describes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will do this in his zeal] or [Yahweh will zealously do this]

33.q: לָ⁠כֵ֗ן כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֶל־מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר לֹ֤א יָבוֹא֙ אֶל־הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֔את וְ⁠לֹֽא־יוֹרֶ֥ה שָׁ֖ם חֵ֑ץ וְ⁠לֹֽא־יְקַדְּמֶ֣⁠נָּה מָגֵ֔ן וְ⁠לֹֽא־יִשְׁפֹּ֥ךְ עֳלֶ֖י⁠הָ סֹלְלָֽה
33.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Therefore Yahweh says about the king of Assyria that he will not come to this city, and he will not shoot an arrow there, and he will not come before it with a shield, and he will not pour out a mound against it]

34.q: בַּ⁠דֶּ֥רֶךְ אֲשֶׁר־בָּ֖א בָּ֣⁠הּ יָשׁ֑וּב וְ⁠אֶל־הָ⁠עִ֥יר הַ⁠זֹּ֛את לֹ֥א יָב֖וֹא נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה
34.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh declares that the king of Assyria will return by the way on which he came, and he will not come to this city]

34.q: בַּ⁠דֶּ֥רֶךְ אֲשֶׁר־בָּ֖א בָּ֣⁠הּ יָשׁ֑וּב וְ⁠אֶל־הָ⁠עִ֥יר הַ⁠זֹּ֛את לֹ֥א יָב֖וֹא
34.note: Yahweh is describing one event before describing another event that would precede it. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened. Alternate translation: [He will not come to this city, but he will return by the way on which he came]

35.q: וְ⁠גַנּוֹתִ֛י עַל־הָ⁠עִ֥יר הַ⁠זֹּ֖את לְ⁠הֽוֹשִׁיעָ֑⁠הּ לְמַֽעֲנִ֔⁠י וּ⁠לְמַ֖עַן דָּוִ֥ד עַבְדִּֽ⁠י
35.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that he will cover over this city to save it, for his own sake and for the sake of David his servant]

Yahweh is speaking as if he were actually going to **cover over** the city of Jerusalem to protect it, as with a shield. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for I will protect this city]
Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [this will happen because]

This verse ends the long first-level quotation that begins at verse 20. It also contains a second-level quotation from Yahweh that concludes at the end of the verse. If you have decided to use punctuation to mark levels of quotation, end this verse with the appropriate punctuation for closing both a second-level and first-level quotation.

36.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [killing 185,000 soldiers]

Isaiah is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [they saw that]

37.q: וַ⁠יִּסַּ֣ע וַ⁠יֵּ֔לֶךְ וַ⁠יָּ֖שָׁב סַנְחֵרִ֣יב מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁ֑וּר וַ⁠יֵּ֖שֶׁב בְּ⁠נִֽינְוֵֽה
37.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could name the king in the earlier part of the sentence and use the pronoun in the later part of the sentence. Alternate translation: [And Sennacherib, the king of Assyria, departed and went, and he returned and stayed in Nineveh]

38.note: The author is using the phrase **And it happened** to introduce a new development within the event of the Assyrians invading Judah. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new development, as modeled by the UST.

Some ancient manuscripts read “and Adrammelech and Sharezer struck him with the sword.” Other ancient manuscripts read “and Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him with the sword.” The ULT follows the reading that includes “his sons.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

The word **and** here indicates a contrast. The sons killed Sennacherib, **and they** themselves **escaped**. If it would be clearer in your language, you can indicate this contrast explicitly. Alternate translation: [and for their part, they escaped]
